name: WILLIS LEASE FINANCE

priced.reason: not a repriceable fcff name or no growth supplied

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: I came into this name expecting to record RICH, because LESSONS already establishes that the capex concept is missing and that correcting it inverts the +209% gap. The adversarial pass is what stopped me, and it found a second defect of comparable size running the other way. The model's synthetic cost of debt for Willis Lease is 19.96% — set by an interest-coverage ratio of EBIT $104.3 million over interest expense $132.1 million, or 0.79x, which for an ENGINE LESSOR is a structural feature of the business rather than distress, because the funding cost of the assets sits below an operating line already struck after their depreciation. The rate Willis actually pays is $132.1 million on $2,320.9 million, or 5.69%. At a 66.7% debt weight that 1,430 basis point error carries the WACC from about 6.9% to 14.02%, and it is the single largest input error on this brief. No flag fires: `speculative_cost_of_debt` only triggers when EBIT is absent or negative, and Willis's is positive.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: The rate Willis Lease actually pays on its debt, against the rate the model assumes — `interest_expense / total_debt` versus `cost_of_debt`, which is the detector the CLVT (2026-09-18) and HP (2026-09-21) entries in LESSONS both nominate.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Yes, entirely, and it changed my verdict. 5.69% paid against 19.96% assumed, at a 66.7% debt weight. Run the grid: at the engine's base and WACC the market requires +6.1%; correcting only the capex takes it to +19.4%; correcting only the WACC takes it to -13.6%; correcting both leaves +1% to +8%. Two large errors in opposite directions give no_edge, not the average and not the half I happened to find first — the SM rule. I would have published RICH on a one-sided correction, and it would have been the mirror of the mistake the 2026-09-01 MFIN pass made when it applied one half of a LESSONS entry without testing the other half.
devils_advocate.unresolved: What owner earnings actually are for an engine lessor that buys and sells engines as its business model. H1 2026 gross fleet purchases were $401.9 million against $302.8 million of sale proceeds, so net investing was only $78.2 million; whether the right base is CFO less GROSS fleet capex (deeply negative), CFO plus NET investing (~$112 million annualised), or something between is an accounting judgment the filings do not settle, and it moves the required growth by fifteen points on its own. I also could not size the August portfolio acquisition's debt, so the $3.47 billion enterprise value is understated by an unknown amount, which makes the name richer than any figure above.

what_changed: Four things since the last pass on this name (2026-08-31), and one of them answers the question that pass could not. (1) THE 2026-08-25 ITEM 2.01 8-K, which the prior pass recorded as unreadable, is the closing of a portfolio acquisition of 12 commercial aircraft and 13 engines — an expansion, not a disposal. (2) Q2 2026 (2026-08-04): revenue $194 million, pre-tax income $38.1 million, adjusted EBITDA $120.7 million (+4.0%), lease rent +6.7% to $77.1 million but core lease rent plus maintenance reserves only +0.5%, net income to common $28.7 million against roughly $59 million. (3) On 2026-09-16 the company signed a $35 million Series B preferred purchase agreement with the Development Bank of Japan at 8.09%, 1,750,000 shares, announced 2026-09-22 — on top of the existing $65 million Series A. (4) A new Willis Engine Repair Center announced for Johor, Malaysia (2026-08-27), with land acquired. Capital is being raised at 8.09% to fund an asset base whose organic revenue line is flat.
consensus_case: At $54.74 Willis Lease is a levered spread business — $2.32 billion of debt and $100 million of preferred against $709 million of book equity — priced on a cycle that has just turned. The bull half is intact: assets under management reached $4.4 billion, up 21%, the company closed a portfolio of 12 aircraft and 13 engines in August, is building a new engine repair centre in Johor, and the spare-engine aftermarket remains structurally short of capacity. The bear half is what the market is reacting to and it is in the Q2 numbers: net income attributable to common fell to $28.7 million from roughly $59 million, core lease rent AND maintenance reserve revenue together grew just 0.5% to $123.6 million, and adjusted EBITDA grew 4.0%. Income from operations of $34.0 million is +20.2%, but a third of pre-tax income is gain on sale of leased equipment ($32.0 million in the quarter). The market is paying for a growing asset base whose organic earnings have stopped growing, funded at 8.09% on the newest preferred.
base_case_rationale: I am not supplying a growth rate, because on this name two defects of comparable size point in OPPOSITE directions and the schema can fix only one of them. The capex concept is missing, which makes the cash-flow base far too high; the synthetic cost of debt is 19.96% against a rate actually paid of 5.69%, which makes the discount rate far too high. Correcting only the base — which is all the schema permits — would price a defensible $211 million of owner earnings through a 14.02% WACC and produce a NEGATIVE fair value of about -$33 a share, which is not a valuation of anything. Across the honest ranges of both inputs the growth the market requires spans -13.6% to +29.0%, and my central estimates (a $211 million base, a WACC of 8-10%) put it at +1% to +8% against a company growing lease rent 6.7% and adjusted EBITDA 4.0%. That is roughly fair, and it is a range, not a number.
key_risks: NO FIGURE ON THIS BRIEF IS USABLE: the capex base is overstated and the discount rate is overstated, by comparable amounts in opposite directions
$2.32B of debt plus $100M of preferred against $709M of book equity, with the newest preferred priced at 8.09% — very little cushion if residual values on CFM56/V2500 assets reprice
Core lease rent plus maintenance reserve revenue grew 0.5% year over year while the asset base grew 21%; the spread is compressing
Roughly a third of pre-tax income is gain on sale of leased equipment ($32.0M in Q2 alone), which is the most cycle-dependent line in the business
The August 2026 portfolio acquisition closed after the 2026-06-30 balance sheet, so enterprise value is understated by whatever funded it
watch_for: Q3 2026 maintenance reserve revenue and utilisation: a third consecutive decline turns a soft patch into a cycle turn
Whether gain on sale of leased equipment holds near $32M a quarter
The FY2026 10-K cash flow statement: gross fleet purchases against sale proceeds, which is the number that decides the owner-earnings base
A corrected capex alias covering lessor equipment purchases AND a cost-of-debt sanity check against the rate actually paid — until both ship, this name cannot be screened
